text: Neither real SDK wants a password passed directly into your code. DefaultAzureCredential and Boto3's own credential chain both search a real, ordered list of sources automatically — and understanding that order is what lets the exact same script run safely on your laptop and in production.

Azure's DefaultAzureCredential checks sources in a real order: environment variables holding a service principal's client ID, tenant ID, and secret; a Managed Identity, when the script happens to be running on an Azure resource — a VM, an App Service, a Function App — that already has one assigned; and finally your own locally signed-in session, from az login or Visual Studio Code.

Notice what's missing from that one line of code: a password. DefaultAzureCredential takes no key, no secret, no argument at all. It walks that same ordered chain every time, and the exact script that runs on your laptop against your az login session runs unchanged in a pipeline or on a VM — only the environment around it decides which source actually wins.

Boto3 runs the same idea for AWS, in its own order: explicit code arguments, which this course avoids entirely; environment variables named AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY; the shared credentials file at tilde slash dot aws slash credentials; and, for a script running on an EC2 instance, an ECS task, or a Lambda function, an IAM role attached directly to that compute resource.

boto3.client, called with just a service name and no key arguments, walks that exact chain automatically. On an EC2 instance with the right IAM role attached, it just works — no key to type, copy, or accidentally commit to source control in the first place.

Both chains exist for the same reason this course's security lessons already made clear: a hardcoded secret sits in a file forever, readable by anyone with access to the repo. Lesson 12 puts both SDKs and this exact authentication pattern to work in one real, complete script that provisions an actual cloud resource.
